    #78432. The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2700 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    The value of combining legal knowledge, technology, workflow design and project management in e-discovery

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.
    • Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.
    • In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I swiftly moved into the world of e-discovery.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 10:47 am CST.

    Ari Kaplan recently spoke with Chantelle Jalland, the associate director of advanced e-discovery and digital services for Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the United States at Ashurst Perkins Coie; and Satinder Soni, the managing director for the United Kingdom at Cimplifi.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Ashurst Perkins Coie.

    In a recent development, chantelle Jalland: I qualified as a lawyer in Australia almost 20 years ago, and when I moved to the U.K., I swiftly moved into the world of e-discovery. At that stage, what attracted me to e-discovery was predictive coding, which meant the machine would learn from those decisions and reduce the need for humans in that really boring manual review phase. When we fast-forward to the release of gen AI, what was incredibly exciting for me was that you could use LLMs to code the documents from a prompt instead of that initial training round. In my current role, I feel incredibly fortunate to work with lawyers who want to use the latest technology to do things differently, so I don’t have to fight like I used to. My remit now at Ashurst Perkins Coie is much broader than e-discovery. I have a team that also builds custom AI solutions across transactional and advisory practice groups, so I very much appreciate the industry recognition moving toward this legal data intelligence.

    Ari Kaplan: Tell us about your background and your role at Cimplifi.

    Industry observers note that satinder Soni: I’ve been in the industry for over 20 years. My career started on the right side of the EDRM model, focusing on courtroom technology, transcription services and evidence presentation in court. E-discovery was just surfacing at that point. It really wasn’t a thing. I then moved into an e-discovery software firm, which was acquired by several conglomerates. I then moved into a global risk consultancy, Control Risks, working with the investigations team on cyber breach investigations, digital forensics and e-discovery. I then moved to Ankura, which took a different approach to e-discovery, focusing more on analytics and subject-matter expertise in construction and turnaround restructuring, forensic accounting and white-collar crime investigations. Then I moved to Cimplifi, a U.S.-based company focused on e-discovery, investigations and contract analytics. They moved to the U.K. almost two years ago. Our U.S. clients had cross-border matters that needed U.K.-based expertise to be compliant with GDPR. We have grown our team here. We have a project management team with diverse professional skills, ranging from consultancies and accountancy firms to technology companies. It’s a great company to be in.

    Ari Kaplan: What’s making e-discovery more complex today, and how is that changing the way you approach each new matter at the outset?

    Sources indicate that chantelle Jalland: One of the biggest challenges is the size of new datasets. We had over 45 terabytes of data for a recent matter. I’ve handled some really large cases before, so this wasn’t the biggest, but given the facts of the case and the scope of the material challenges in the dispute, I expected the volume to be much smaller. It was a surprise, based on the facts, that it was that large, and it was simply the product of more data being created today. We also have platform switching. This morning, I was on a call with a colleague about a particular client matter, then received an email on the matter to an external party, then I had some internal Teams chat messages, and in one of those messages, they also shared a live document with status updates. That was all within a few minutes, so everything was moving so much faster, and there were four different sources of information on one particular matter or glitch. If you think about that and expand it, if every single person is just adding this tiny bit of additional information, it’s going to lead to a data explosion. That’s also the biggest opportunity because the large matters are the ones that are interesting and exciting. They’ve got things that will go wrong or problems, and you want those differences to make it more interesting and something new to solve.

    Ari Kaplan: What e-discovery challenges do your clients most often ask you to solve?

    Satinder Soni: Everything has a different variable, and each e-discovery matter is a challenge because it is a reactive industry. Our clients come in quite hard and fast, and we have to take a step back to understand the data scoping. I have a separate challenge where they underestimate how much data there is, so you have to ease the shock of what it’s actually going to cost. But if you apply the right technology, phase it out, structure the workflow and talk them through it, the challenge then is pacing it, being realistic and providing timelines. The latest challenge really is applying AI into their workflows and driving the mindset shift they need to use a different type of analytics. They’ve just gotten used to CAL, and there is a bit of fatigue with it being more efficient and more cost-effective. We say it with every upcoming tool we bring in, and the challenge is always the mindset shift.

    Ari Kaplan: The Ashurst Perkins Coie Advanced Legal Solutions offering combines legal knowledge, technology, workflow design, project management and flexible resourcing. How does that combination enhance client service, and how do you define success before the work begins?

    Chantelle Jalland: There’s tremendous value in having multiple service offerings under one roof. We also have our risk advisory or consulting arm, which enables us to undertake deep data analytics tasks, and this gives us what we refer to internally as our triple threat. We have Advance, our fresh law arm, risk advisory and our core services team. Before the work begins, much of the success comes back to those foundational principles, and it builds on what Sati mentioned about managing expectations on timelines and being realistic. Historically, a partner will promise a client that we will deliver something in a certain amount of time for a certain cost, and that promise may not be realistic because the scope fundamentally changes or the expectation isn’t technically possible within the timeframe. They didn’t understand the basic principle that if you don’t understand the component, you can’t advise in that area, and that’s where we bring the right people into the conversation earlier. We have that open conversation and set small milestones or goals, so we’re meeting our client’s expectations along the way. And like everyone, I take great pride in an accurate cost estimate. But really, that data can expand at a different rate compared to a previous matter that you might have done an estimate on, or there’s a subset of data that’s got a processing error. There are so many things that can vary from what you might expect. As it shifts, it’s about having that conversation and letting everyone know it’s different from the original ask, and what I’ve found is clients appreciate that openness and willingness to have the conversation. You are advising, and there’s a lot more respect for the advice and the experience that can be offered in this area.

    Ari Kaplan: Where are clients rethinking their approach most often, understanding their data earlier, managing review, coordinating providers, or generally adjusting their litigation strategy?

    Satinder Soni: All of the above. E-discovery is a complex process. I’ve seen it where you’ve got your litigation strategy set, then you do the data scoping piece, and then you look at the early data and assess it. And when the review is happening, that’s when they realize we’re missing a custodian or this data source. Then the litigation strategy has to be readjusted. Then we go back to the data assessment. It can expand into other litigation support service lines, like asset tracing, or you need a forensic accountant. Chantelle put it really well. Communication is key. Understanding your stakeholders is part of that. Setting realistic timelines is part of that. It flits between the litigation strategy and understanding your data and that feedback loop.

    Ari Kaplan: What needs to happen earlier in a matter for a legal team, the e-discovery team and a service provider to work most effectively together?

    Chantelle Jalland: We tend to manage matters in-house with our legal team, but we also work with service providers on some matters. Sometimes a client has a preexisting relationship with a preferred provider, or we choose to engage a service provider due to their expertise. We recently had a matter involving historic offline databases that were in the format of a decommissioned product, so we needed to convert them for a current document review platform. It was more efficient to use an existing solution, rather than script something custom for that matter. What needs to happen to work effectively together is to get on a call early with all the right people. You can cut through so much with a phone call, making sure everyone is working toward the same strategy from the outset.

    Ari Kaplan: When your team is engaged by a client under pressure, what distinguishes a trusted adviser from a provider that simply executes instructions?

    Satinder Soni: You should never be an order taker. Just because the client indicates it, doesn’t mean it’s always the right thing. They come to us because we are experts in the field. They trust us to guide and support them through the process. Often, it goes wrong when the client calls, and everyone’s excited, and they dive right in, applying the same methodology from the previous project. Take a step back. Standard information to ask for at the beginning includes e-data, what has happened, the discovery objective, the goals they’re trying to achieve, and the timeline they’re working toward. Review data types, nonstandard files, foreign languages and whether the data is structured or unstructured. Really get into the details that will influence the e-discovery project and help it achieve its goals. We advise gathering as much information as possible in advance, so we can choose the right technology, manage timelines and predict accurate costs. In those instances, accurate cost prediction is also key. Our job as a trusted adviser is to say, “We can save costs if we do it this way.”.

    Ari Kaplan: Where is AI making the most meaningful difference in your work today, and where is its promise still a bit ahead of its practical value?

    It has been revealed that chantelle Jalland: AI has meaningfully changed my work. From a personal productivity perspective, AI call summaries make follow-up emails and meeting organization much easier. When I check a draft email, there are several small examples I use every day. On a larger scale, for high-impact matters, we have seen really effective use in due diligence, whether it’s legislative reviews for businesses or from an advisory perspective. The area where I see the most promise is large-scale document reviews. We are using AI for document review in a way that replaces CAL. So you filter down, you get a set of, say, 20,000 documents, and run it through. It is more effective than traditional manual review. It’s more effective than CAL. However, I see huge leaps ahead when it comes to document review. Most excitingly, I think, coming back to what Sati stated earlier about working in a reactive industry, we are doing everything later. It’s actually about bringing those AI use cases further forward. Within a corporation, it’s about tracking themes, using the data more effectively, so you can identify the last 10 litigation matters or regulatory investigations that are actually costing you money, analyze that data, and then try to prevent future matters. That’s where it’s really exciting.

    Ari Kaplan: When would you choose not to use AI in a litigation support matter?

    Satinder Soni: We should all be using it in some way, shape or form. Traditionally, it was suggested that not all matters needed AI or analytics, either because it was cost-prohibitive, the dataset wasn’t compatible, or there wasn’t enough data to perform analysis. Recently, we’ve seen a shift toward using AI on small matters, such as DSARs. I have seen clients use AI on DSARs, and it seems effective. It frees up time for project managers to do more thoughtful work because DSARs don’t really go anywhere. They’re weaponized most of the time. So if they’re using it on investigation and litigation matters, their time is better spent. This is where AI can be used thoughtfully. There are still alternatives. CAL is being phased out, but it’s still there and still serves as a bridge to advising against linear review. But if people are not yet comfortable using AI, which hopefully they are, it’s in your everyday work now, so I just think, piece by piece, they’re trying it. I can’t think of any instance of not using AI.

    Ari Kaplan: As we leverage technology to perform more work, which human skills become increasingly valuable, and how do you develop them within your team?

    According to recent reports, chantelle Jalland: Communication is hugely crucial, so it’s something I’m focusing on from a recruitment perspective. We have to think about which skills can be taught and which are harder to teach. There’s analytical thinking. We need to make sure that the advisory stage isn’t so automated or process-driven that it’s replaced by AI. It’s about understanding that judgment is still needed and how to apply it. AI will be useful in many contexts, but how you use it will vary by use case. The risk is quite high if you don’t check the outputs, for example. It’s also about making sure people understand that risk. When it comes to training, it’s not a one-and-done. It’s continuous, and the same is true for communication. In a global law firm, different teams adopt different styles, and what works for one team doesn’t work for another. It’s about continuous learning without people feeling fatigued by constant learning.

    Ari Kaplan: What are the hallmarks of great client service in an AI-enabled environment?

    In a recent development, satinder Soni: Great client service is all about communication, even when it’s bad news. Hopefully, it’s never bad news, but when it is, pick up the phone and have a conversation. We’ve gone crazy with short-form messaging, and what can be stated in 10 emails can be said in a five-minute conversation. Then, with AI, be thoughtful about how we’re using it. Don’t fall into the trap of using AI for everything, and keep learning. There is a job you need to do: Put clients first, break down tasks, add structure to your work, and don’t just let AI take control.

    Ari Kaplan: How do you see e-discovery and legal tech evolving?

    Chantelle Jalland: I am very positive and optimistic about the future of e-discovery. There are many opportunities because, essentially, all the button-clicking will be gone soon, which is a great opportunity for people who work in e-discovery. You can apply a wide range of tools. It’s not just one technology. There are MCP connectors that you can use to adapt to certain platforms. So you are going to have so much more flexibility in the options. It does create more risk, potentially, if you’re not following a standard protocol, but what is exciting is that you can differentiate yourself in the market by specializing in solutions for certain use cases. Going back to first principles: understanding the problem, how you’re going to solve it, and considering all your options. It’s not going to be as linear. In the next five years, I would even say in the next year, we will be having a very different conversation about workflows in particular.

    Listen to the complete interview at Reinventing Professionals.

    Ari Kaplan regularly interviews leaders in the legal industry and in the broader professional services community to share perspective, highlight transformative change and introduce fresh technology at his blog and on Apple Podcasts.

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    • According to recent reports, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • We’re looking for a Data API Engineer to join our Data API Team and help improve the feature set, reliability and performance of our Data API, based on the PostgREST project.
    • This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Data API Engineer to join our Data API Team and help improve the feature set, reliability and performance of our Data API, based on the PostgREST project.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Work on PostgREST’s PostgreSQL driver (based on Hasql) and remove bottlenecks and improve it’s performance.

    Work on PostgREST development of newly introduced features and bug fixes, aligned towards the goal of a multitenant Data API.

    Resolve incidents and escalated support challenges, while also improving observability and performance.

    Collaborate cross-functionally with other teams to debug and solve integration complications with the Supabase platform.

    Strong Haskell skills with at least 3 years of experience.

    Experience using the C language.

    Solid knowledge of SQL and plpgsql scripting in PostgreSQL.

    Strong track record of contributing to and engaging with open-source projects. Bonus points if you’ve maintained an open source project.

    Strong experience with providing technical support to owners with varying levels of technical expertise.

    Experience with debugging applications under the Linux operating system.

    It has been revealed that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Recent findings suggest that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    In a recent development, once a year, the entire organization gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Recent findings suggest that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    • The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec.
    • According to recent reports, in United States v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

    The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

    According to recent reports, in United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

    Industry observers note that in the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”.

    The challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”.

    Industry observers note that in another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a Upcoming York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

    Trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”.

    The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

    And in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the Latest York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

    Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

    With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi stated, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

    Bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of Latest York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”.

    According to recent reports, when challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the Latest York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

    In addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:.

    Industry observers note that one thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

    Finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth. More than 9 million developers and 250,000+ customers now build on Supabase, and the majority of new databases on the platform are created by AI app builders — so the systems underneath have to stay reliable while they grow fast.

    Sources indicate that container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of. We own cluster lifecycle and cluster classes, multi-cluster and multi-region topology, capacity, scheduling, isolation and runtime safety, the higher-level platform APIs, the Kubernetes deployment contract and Argo semantics, rollout primitives, and runtime configuration and secret injection.

    Your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it. This is not a gatekeeper role. You'll make the reliable path the easy path: building the automation and platform APIs that let product teams run safely by default, instrumenting what we operate, and making sure that when something breaks we detect it and recover fast.

    The work spans three strength areas:.

    Tooling & ecosystem — deep knowledge of the container and orchestration landscape (Kubernetes, containerd/OCI, the CNCF ecosystem) and a clear point of view on how to compose it.

    Software engineering — designing and building the platform's automation, controllers, and internal tooling as production code, including solutions that don't come pre-shaped by an existing tool.

    Operational / SRE practice — the discipline (SLOs, error budgets, incident response, ORRs) that runs the platform at scale as a predictable one.

    We expect you to be genuinely deep in at least one of these, and many of our strongest candidates are deep in two (usually leaning toward one). Bringing real strength across all three is rare and exceptional — and even then, no one is equally strong in all three at once, so you'd focus where you're most needed at any given time. Different profiles are welcome here; tell us which of these is your center of gravity.

    Regardless of the skill set, all team members carry a share of the team's on-call rota, responding to platform incidents and driving them to resolution and follow-up.

    Platform reliability & operations.

    Define SLIs/SLOs and error budgets for the container platform itself, and build error-budget policies that actually gate platform changes.

    Own the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process for latest platform capabilities and major changes.

    Design and track metrics for platform uptime, and increase observability into the platform by capturing the right metrics, logs, and traces across the platform layers.

    Drive the incident-to-improvement pipeline: facilitate blameless postmortems, connect findings to readiness gaps, spot repeat failure patterns, and push through systemic fixes.

    Build and maintain the platform's automation, controllers, operators, and internal tooling — writing production code and shipping it, not just wiring together existing tools.

    Design and implement the platform-side CI/CD and rollout primitives that speed up platform deployments while working within proper change and release management.

    Implement and maintain security automation for the platform: intrusion detection, automated remediation, and patch management.

    Identify and quantify operational toil, and build the automation that removes it rather than just documenting it.

    Contribute to the platform's continual testing automation — the test suites and pipelines that validate platform releases are fit for purpose before they reach tenants.

    Tooling, ecosystem & architecture.

    Act as a platform reliability and architecture expert — contribute to failure-mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design for multi-tenant container workloads.

    Evaluate and evolve the platform's tooling ecosystem (orchestration, runtime, networking, isolation, and observability stack) with a clear, opinionated view on trade-offs.

    Improve system architecture to reduce infrastructure cost while balancing security, reliability, and performance across tenants.

    Guide teams building on the platform to design sustainable on-call practices for their own services: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction.

    Have 5+ years in platform engineering, container/Kubernetes platform operations, SRE, or production infrastructure, and have operated production systems at scale and carried on-call for them.

    Are genuinely deep in at least one — ideally two — of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):.

    It has been revealed that tooling & ecosystem — know the container/orchestration landscape well: Kubernetes, containerd and the OCI/CRI standards, and the surrounding CNCF ecosystem (e.g. Argo CD/Argo Rollouts for GitOps and progressive delivery; Cilium/eBPF networking and the Gateway API; Karpenter/KEDA-style autoscaling; and workload-isolation runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers).     AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    2026 Year in Review: When AI dominated the room

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to fresh technology faster than ever before.
    • Sources indicate that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors.
    • It was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to fresh technology faster than ever before. At the same time, technology has advanced exponentially, with artificial intelligence changing how information is obtained and how work gets done.

    Sources indicate that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors. Meanwhile, AI startups proliferated across the legal technology landscape, with some disappearing overnight, while others were snapped up and acquired less than a year after launch.

    It was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up. From tracking updated software features and emerging AI-powered technologies to learning how to use AI ethically, lawyers had a lot on their plates. That’s where my 2026 columns came in. Each one offered a summary of the latest legal technology news or provided roadmaps for legal software adoption in law firms.

    According to recent reports, trusts and estates lawyers rely on drafting software to create complex planning documents and manage related estate work. These tools include features like guided interviews, automated forms and shared client information that support document creation and reduce drafting errors. Some software also helps lawyers customize plans and handle tasks such as trust funding and estate administration. Understanding how the options differ can assist lawyers in choosing the software that fits their trusts and estates practice’s workflows.

    Recent findings suggest that AI systems reflect the assumptions and perspectives of the people who develop them, as well as the data used to train them. Those assumptions can shape AI outputs and reinforce bias, especially when women and other underrepresented groups have little input into how systems are designed. Drawing on the Women + AI Summit, including more perspectives when developing AI matters; it can impact the questions considered, improve outcomes, and determine how these systems affect users and the public at large.

    At Legalweek 2026, agentic AI and the competition to become law firms’ central AI platform were recurring themes. There were also plenty of updates from legal technology providers, from platforms that connected research, drafting and firm data to specialized tools for e-discovery, litigation, legal research and skills training. The conference announcements highlight how companies are building both integrated ecosystems and focused applications that help lawyers incorporate newly introduced AI-driven workflows into their firms.

    Drawing on findings from the 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report, this column examines how the profession is responding to rapid AI adoption, access-to-justice hurdles and concerns about the rule of law. The report demonstrates that individual AI use has grown faster than the implementation of firm policies and training, even as survey respondents see technology as one way of bridging the access-to-justice moat. Also notable was that lawyers were most concerned about the rule of law and its continued degradation.

    In a recent development, the growing number of court filings with fabricated or inaccurate case citations has led to a fresh category of tools designed to check AI-generated legal documents. Citation checkers can help identify false citations, misquoted language and inaccurate descriptions of case holdings. There are citation-checking tools built into drafting platforms in addition to those found in stand-alone applications, with a focus on their capabilities and costs. Before investing in a new tool, consider whether the time saved through AI research, drafting and citation checking justifies the expense or whether traditional research and drafting may ultimately be more cost-effective.

    As AI takes on routine work traditionally assigned to junior lawyers, it may also reduce opportunities to develop practical legal skills. Training platforms can allow law students and early-career lawyers to build experience through courtroom simulations, interactive exercises and AI- or VR-based practice. These tools allow users to rehearse tasks, such as deposition questioning, negotiation and courtroom advocacy, with some offering immediate performance feedback. Using these simulation-based learning platforms, recent law school graduates are better able to bridge the experiential gap and ensure that they have the building blocks needed to thrive in the AI era.

    Partnerships and integrations dominated the news at ILTACON 2026, as legal technology companies worked to connect their AI tools with legal data, software and workflows. In addition to those developments, there were newly introduced products that streamlined litigation, legal writing and law firm pricing. The conference takeaway was that legal AI is moving beyond stand-alone tools toward connected systems, for better or for worse.

    Sources indicate that litigation teams often work with large, complex collections of digital evidence, which can be difficult to organize and analyze using traditional methods. AI-powered fact analysis tools can assist with the review of case materials by identifying people, events and inconsistencies and by creating timelines that link to supporting documents. These tools can help litigators analyze and understand the evidence and collaborate more efficiently with their teams.

    As fresh AI-powered platforms enter the market, solo and small-firm lawyers now have more affordable options for legal research. There are some tools priced at $100 or less per month that lawyers can use to swiftly and easily search caselaw and statutes. Some also offer case analysis and citation-checking tools to confirm subsequent case treatment. These platforms provide smaller practices with more options, but lawyers should still weigh the cost and accuracy rates against existing research tools, along with the time required to verify AI-generated results.

She is the nationally recognized author of Cloud Computing for Lawyers and is a co-author of Social Media for Lawyers: The Next Frontier, both published by the American Bar Association.     An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences.
    • Sources indicate that iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct.
    • In a recent development, the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

    Sources indicate that iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

    In a recent development, the state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

    Sources indicate that in two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”.

    In addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

    Within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

    It has been revealed that having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

    Industry observers note that last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

    The solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

    Industry observers note that but the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead said he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

    Once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

    César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

    Recommended Citation: César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/an-election-impact-on-the-supreme-courts-immigration-docket/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A recent Upcoming York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

    In a recent development, the city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. Fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani intends to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

    “The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

    Additionally, the upcoming law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

    “Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani remarked.

    Bloomberg Law and MSN had coverage.

    #78415. The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    The Supreme Court before it stood apart

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A.
    • In her excellent fresh book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.
    • According to recent reports, that will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press).

    In her excellent fresh book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

    According to recent reports, that will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history demonstrates that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

    In a recent development, shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

    Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

    But this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

    According to recent reports, chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

    It has been revealed that marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

    Justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

    Nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political issues as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

    According to recent reports, and in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

    To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The Upcoming York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

    Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

    Industry observers note that shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of New York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

    Justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

    Justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

    Again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

    Just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

    According to recent reports, during Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to issue a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

    Sources indicate that when Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

    Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

    It has been revealed that in the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a new story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.).

    Recent findings suggest that if I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

    Regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

    Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation.

    Sources indicate that recommended Citation: Mark Miller, The Supreme Court before it stood apart, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-before-it-stood-apart/.

    It has been revealed that PASADENA, Calif. (CN) â A Boozefighterâs latest battle in Southern California has little to do with booze or barroom brawls.

    Instead, it is a First and Second Amendment fight over whether San Diego County Sheriff Kelly Martinez can revoke Kenneth Shilling’s license to carry concealed weapons because of his association with what she believes is a criminal street gang, the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club.

    On Friday, a Ninth Circuit panel revived Shillingâs lawsuit against Martinez, finding a lower court erred in dismissing the action against the sheriff and San Diego County.

    According to recent reports, shilling received his license to carry concealed weapons in June 2022 under the previous sheriff. However, his license was revoked by Martinez in December 2023 under a clause in the California penal code requiring âgood moral character.".

    In a recent development, writing in a unanimous decision, U.S. Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay found that Shilling sufficiently claimed his right to free association had been infringed after the sheriff deprived him of his Second Amendment right.

    âIn dismissing this claim, the district court misunderstood the nature of the free association right,â Bumatay, a Donald Trump appointee, wrote. âIt asserted that Shilling had to show the revocation of his CCW license somehow prevented him from associating with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club or participating in the clubâs activities. While preventing an individual from participating in a groupâs lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, itâs infringed in âvaried ways.ââ.

    The three-judge panel found Martinez was acting as a policymaker, rather than a state official, in her revocation of Shillingâs license under the good moral character requirement.

    âNo state law mandated this county-specific definition,â Bumatay continued. âIn other words, the county of San Diego â not California â made association with the Boozefighters a basis to revoke a CCW license.â.

    Bumatay was joined by U.S. Circuit Judge Kenneth Lee, another Trump appointee, and U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung, a Joe Biden appointee.

    “The Bill of Rightâs prevails over politics,” attorney Gary Gorski, representing Shilling, noted in an email to Courthouse News.

    Sources indicate that the good moral character requirement in the stateâs penal code was replaced with more objective and defined criteria in January 2024, shortly after the revocation of Shillingâs license, following the Supreme Courtâs decision in Latest York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.

    Shilling filed the lawsuitin June 2024.

    In his complaint, he described the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club as an organization that is more involved in charitable events than its historical status might suggest. The organization was founded in Los Angeles in 1946 by returning World War II veterans seeking camaraderie over their shared love of motorcycle riding.

    The organization claims it has never been an outlaw motorcycle gang or part of the â1%â of motorcycle clubs that operate outside mainstream riding activities.

    Shilling, a resident of Chula Vista, California, has been a longtime employee at the Chula Vista Elementary School District. He has no criminal history, the panel wrote.

    Reinsurer TIG found liable over Libby Mine asbestos exposure claims

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Courthousenews

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.
    • (CN) â An eight-person federal jury found reinsurer TIG liable after Omaha-based National Indemnity claimed TIG didn’t fully cover a sweeping payout for widespread contamination from the Libby Mine asbestos exposure.
    • In a recent development, jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.

    OMAHA, Neb. (CN) â An eight-person federal jury found reinsurer TIG liable after Omaha-based National Indemnity claimed TIG didn’t fully cover a sweeping payout for widespread contamination from the Libby Mine asbestos exposure.

    In a recent development, jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG. They awarded National Indemnity $39.2 million in indemnity, $3.2 million in prejudgment interest, $21.1 million in postjudgment interest and $16.1 million in expenses.

    They declined to award National Indemnity any future defense costs.

    Attorneys for both sides declined to comment after the verdict was read.

    National Indemnity Insurance Company turned to TIG Insurance Company and other reinsurers after agreeing in 2022, with Montana, to resolve all coverage claims over asbestos exposure from the mine since the 1960s for $157 million.

    National Indemnity insured the state from July 1, 1973, to July 1, 1975; TIG provided the company’s reinsurance at that time.

    TIG claimed National Indemnity did not offer adequate evidence and billed amounts not covered by the reinsurance agreement, essentially finagling the numbers to make TIG cover part of the massive bill.

    âIt lied," said Scott L. Davis, a Dallas-based attorney for the Spencer Fane firm, representing TIG, speaking of National Indemnity during closing arguments late Thursday afternoon.

    National Indemnity said it kept TIG informed throughout the claims process, but the reinsurer never got involved, something it had a right to do.

    “They could have helped; they didnât,” Michael Knoerzer, a Fresh York-based attorney for Clyde & Co., representing National Indemnity, told the jury Thursday. âItâs undisputed in this case they never asked.â.

    In 2004, the state of Montana was found liable for asbestos risk to miners and residents near Libby, a small city in the state’s northwest.

    From 1963 to 1990, W.R. Grace & Co. extracted vermiculite at the mine, about 7 miles outside of Libby. Vermiculite, once commonly used for fireproof roofing, insulation and wallpaper, is not dangerous. But the asbestos the mining stirred up was.

    It has been revealed that decades of widespread asbestos contamination from the mine caused the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare its first-ever public health emergency during a 2009 Superfund cleanup.

    In a recent development, thousands of W.R. Grace workers, their families and residents since the 1960s have been injured or died from lung disease related to working at or living near the mine.

    The fight over who should be held liable started about 2000, shortly after reports of workers falling ill sparked an emergency cleanup. Contamination has since been blamed for hundreds of deaths.

    Sources indicate that reinsurance is dubbed âinsurance for insurance companiesâ by the Reinsurance Association of America. Under reinsurance, one insurance company indemnifies another for a loss the company buying the policy cannot handle alone â something that National Indemnity claims TIG did not fully do.

    According to recent reports, after the $157 million payout, National Indemnity billed its reinsurers more than $101 million. They did not pay. Since first filing the lawsuit in 2022, all other reinsurers except TIG have been dropped from the suit. TIG has paid National Indemnity what it believed it owed â $12.7 million.

    According to National Indemnity, the insurance contract required National Indemnity to pay as much as $3 million per loss, with unlimited occurrences. At first, the state mentioned 21 occurrences involved state inspectors not warning miners about the asbestos risk.

    But National Indemnity feared that, with potentially thousands of miners and locals affected by asbestos exposure, the number of occurrences could multiply as the matter moved again through Montana courts, with the state Supreme Court telling the parties to litigate the number of occurrences.

    Ultimately, National Indemnity and the state settled at 27 occurrences. At $3 million apiece, the bill came to $81 million. The roughly $76 million remaining largely came from past and present defense costs.

    According to recent reports, under their contract, TIG was responsible for one-third of National Indemnityâs costs. So, according to National Indemnity, it would have to pay $1 million for each occurrence.

    Montana and National Indemnity counted each failure to warn by the state as an occurrence. At matter is whether individual deaths could also count as an occurrence. National Indemnity argued it could have found itself on the hook for âbillionsâ if individual deaths were counted, which led it to settle at 27.

    In her instructions to the jury Thursday, U.S. District Judge Susan M. Bazis stated National Indemnity would have to prove, by greater weight of evidence, that it performed its obligation under the contract and that TIG breached it, causing damages to the Omaha-based insurer.

    Industry observers note that the Joe Biden appointee mentioned TIG agreed there was adequate proof of 21 occurrences. National Indemnity would have to prove it provided satisfactory evidence of each occurrence to TIG.

    “By greater weight of the evidence” is a less strict standard than the “beyond a reasonable doubt” standard in criminal cases. As in criminal cases, the jury selects a foreperson, and the vote must be unanimous.

    • The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.
    • According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

    Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

    According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

    “Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”.

    “A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

    Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

    “The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s vital to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith mentioned to Law.com.

    Recent findings suggest that smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

    According to recent reports, “We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith stated. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s vital to look at their options early.”.
